newsitem.title: USA: Jackson stumps for Clinton, turnout in Florida.
newsitem.headline: Jackson stumps for Clinton, turnout in Florida.

text.p: Civil rights leader Jesse Jackson said on Monday he had no regrets over his decision not to seek the White House and is supporting President Clinton because he has been "fundamentally a good president."

"I think I made the right decision. I support Bill Clinton," the African American political leader told Reuters in a telephone interview during a day spent at rallies across the state to encourage voter turnout on Nov. 5.

Though Jackson disagreed with Clinton's signing of the controversial welfare bill over the summer, he praised the president's preservation of affirmative action, support for a ban on assault weapons and increase in the minimum wage.
"He's been fundamentally a good president. And I support him," he said.
Some observers have said that Republican nominee Bob Dole's choice of Jack Kemp as his running mate might win him black voters who might otherwise have voted Democratic.
But Jackson said he disagreed, saying Kemp had backed off positions considered generally favourable to African-Americans since joining the Republican ticket.

"He's gotten a lot of miles out of one idea," Jackson said, referring to Kemp's support for "Enterprise Zones," to promote business development in inner cities. On affirmative action, Jackson said of Kemp, "He betrayed his convictions ... He simply had a priority to join that ticket and to embrace an ideology he doesn't even believe in."

Florida is the fourth biggest state, with 25 electoral votes. Though it has gone to the Republicans in nine of the past 11 presidential elections, Clinton lost Florida to President George Bush in 1992 by only about 100,000 votes, despite spending little time or money in the state. Polls have given him a narrow lead in Florida this year.
Jackson's tour of the state on Monday included stops in Daytona Beach, Orlando and Tampa, before heading to the southern part of the state on Tuesday.
Jackson said he hoped turnout would be high, noting he had addressed a crowd of 1,500 in Daytona Beach on Monday morning and then another 2,000 people outside Orlando at mid-day.
